deep.reconstruction:
Context (E477, 1776): Euler studies the double sums q^m := Σ_{x≥1} x^{-m}(1 + 2^{-n} + … + x^{-n}), with m+n = w. The inner partial sum includes x itself, so in modern terms q^m = ζ*(m,n) = ζ(m,n) + ζ(w), a multiple zeta-star value. Euler's p^w stands for ζ(w). Inside an order w, 'p^k' (k<w) abbreviates the product ζ(k)ζ(w−k), and a bare 'p' stands for the formal, divergent product ζ(1)ζ(w−1). The asterisk marks a missing term.

Top of the page: Euler completes the list for weight w = 11, which began on the previous page:
- q^6 = 463/2 ζ(11) − 126 ζ(2)ζ(9) − 21 ζ(4)ζ(7)
- q^5 = −461/2 ζ(11) + 126 ζ(2)ζ(9) + 21 ζ(4)ζ(7) + ζ(5)ζ(6)
- …
- q^2 = 28 ζ(11) − 8 ζ(2)ζ(9) − 2 ζ(3)ζ(8) − 6 ζ(4)ζ(7) − 4 ζ(5)ζ(6)

§31: Euler then examines the coefficients a_k of ζ(w) in q^{w−k}, for each odd order w = 5, 7, 9, 11. He finds a first-order recurrence, verified in four columns:
- a_1 = (w+1)/2;
- k·a_k = (w+1−k)·a_{k−1} + (−1)^{k+1}(w+1)/2, for k = 2, …, w−1.

The last step involves q^1 = ζ*(1, w−1), which diverges. Euler writes it formally:
- w = 11: q = −5ζ(11) + ζ(1)ζ(10) + ζ(2)ζ(9) + … + ζ(5)ζ(6)
- w = 9 and w = 7: analogous, with leading coefficients −4 and −3.

This is exactly the stuffle-regularised value: ζ*(1,n) = ζ(1)ζ(n) − ζ*(n,1) + ζ(n+1).

§32 announces using the recurrence to predict order 13. The next page carries this out (A = 7, B = 77/2, C = 287/2, …).

Modern closed form: the coefficient of ζ(w) in ζ*(s, w−s), w odd, is ((−1)^s·C(w,s) + 1)/2. Equivalently, in ζ(s,t) it is ((−1)^s·C(w,s) − 1)/2, which is the ζ(w) term of the Borwein–Borwein–Girgensohn (1995) formula for odd-weight double zeta values. Euler's recurrence follows from this, since k·C(w,k) = (w+1−k)·C(w,k−1).

Checks:
- Every recurrence line on the page is arithmetically correct (e.g. 5·463/2 = 7·329/2 + 6 and 6·461/2 = 6·463/2 − 6).
- The pairs q^s + q^{w−s} = ζ(s)ζ(w−s) + ζ(w) (the stuffle relation) hold for all the weight-11 formulas.
- q^10 agrees with Euler's classical ζ(n,1) formula.
- The leading coefficients agree with ((−1)^s·C(11,s) + 1)/2: 6, −27, 83, −329/2, 463/2, −461/2, 331/2, −82, 28, −5.

The page belongs to Euler's well-known demonstration that all odd-weight double sums reduce to ζ(w) and products ζ(a)ζ(w−a).
errors: For m+n = 5 the print appears to read 'q = 2p^5 + p + p^2'. Alternation of signs, the recurrence (4·2 = 2·11/2 − 3) and stuffle regularisation all require q^1 = −2ζ(5) + ζ(1)ζ(4) + ζ(2)ζ(3). The minus sign is missing or illegible in the print.
In the w = 11 line 'est enim q = −5p + p + …' the exponent 11 on the first p is missing in print; it should be −5p^{11}.
In the w = 7 line the last term is printed like 'p^8'; it should be p^3 (i.e. ζ(3)ζ(4)). This is a typographical slip.

ideas.what: Explicit evaluation of the weight-11 double sums ζ*(s, 11−s) in terms of ζ(11) and products ζ(a)ζ(11−a)
ideas.modern_name: Reduction of odd-weight double zeta values (Euler / Borwein–Borwein–Girgensohn theorem)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E477), proved in general by Borwein, Borwein and Girgensohn (1995) and by Huard, Williams and Zhang (1996)

ideas.what: Recurrence k·a_k = (w+1−k)·a_{k−1} ± (w+1)/2 for the coefficient of ζ(w), used to extrapolate to weight 13
ideas.modern_name: Coefficient ((−1)^s·C(w,s) ± 1)/2 in the BBG odd-weight formula
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (empirical); the closed form is in Borwein–Borwein–Girgensohn 1995

ideas.what: Formal treatment of the divergent q^1 = ζ*(1, w−1) using a symbolic product ζ(1)ζ(w−1)

missed.claim: Euler extends the table of double sums to the divergent case m = 1, writing it with a formal ζ(1)ζ(w−1) term. The values he records coincide exactly with the stuffle-regularised values, and he feeds them into the same recurrence as the convergent ones. This is an early instance of harmonic-product regularisation. It is rarely mentioned in historical accounts of MZV regularisation.
missed.quote: est enim q = -5p + p + p^2 + p^3 + p^4 + p^5
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is of historical interest only: it shows Euler implicitly working with the stuffle-regularised algebra. Mathematically it is well understood today.

deep.surprise_reason: The results (odd-weight double zeta reduction and its binomial coefficients) are well known and credited to Euler's E477. The only mildly notable point is the consistent formal regularisation of the divergent m = 1 case.
transcription_corrections: In the m+n = 7 column the print shows 'q = -3p^7 + p + p^2 + p^8'; the last term is p^3 (a printer's slip).
In the m+n = 5 column the transcription gives 'q = 2p^5 + p + p^2'; mathematically it should be '-2p^5' (the sign is missing or faint in print).
